body.heading: Make it a performance, not a lecture
paragraphs: A tidy-up song does two jobs: it tells everyone the tidy has started, and it tells them when it ends. Choose something short and cheerful — two or three minutes — and make it the official song, played for no other purpose. Children move differently to music; most of us do.
The timer version works the same way: 'can we beat the clock?' Set five minutes, visible, and let the room race it. The finish line matters more than the standard reached.

body.heading: Sort into few, big categories
paragraphs: Young children tidy well when the categories are big and physical: things that live in this room in the basket, things that belong elsewhere in the basket by the door, rubbish in the bin. Fine sorting is an adult hobby; do not let it slow the song down.
Label baskets with pictures if readers are few. A basket that announces itself gets filled.

body.heading: Stop when the song stops
paragraphs: When the music ends, tidying ends, even if the room is only better rather than perfect. Keeping that promise is what makes children start willingly next time. A room at eighty percent, achieved cheerfully and often, beats a perfect room achieved by nagging.
Change the official song now and then, by vote. A tidy-up with a new soundtrack feels like a new game, and the choosing is part of the fun.

description: One short song, one timer, big simple categories: tidying that children will actually join in with.
